en: A Compendium of All Doctrines:
An Investigation of the Means of Valid Cognition.
In this context, valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is correct experience.
The inclusion of the term "correct" is for the purpose of excluding doubt and error.
Among these, doubt is a cognition that lacks definitive determination.
For example: "Is this a post or a person? and so forth.
Erroneous determination (*mithyādhyavasāya*) is error (*viparyaya*);
for example: "There are two moons," and so forth.
The term "experience" (anubhava) is included for the purpose of excluding memory (smṛti).
Memory is a cognition produced solely from a latent impression (saṃskāra),
such as "this is my mother," and so forth.
Latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) is the impression (*saṃskāra*) of past experience.
And that, being awakened by the sight of a similar object, is the cause of memory.
But how is it that by the mention of "experience" (*anubhava*), memory (*smṛti*) is excluded?
Because knowledge other than memory is experience.
As they say: "Experience is the means of valid cognition; it is that which is other than memory.
By the word *mātra* (only) in the phrase "arising from memory-impression alone" (*saṃskāramātraja*), recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is excluded.
Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is the knowledge arising from both mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and sensory contact,
such as "this is that very same jar.
Now, if experience alone constitutes valid cognition (*pramā*), why is there a conventional usage of the term "valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) regarding scripture and the like?
We say it is precisely because it generates valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

As it was stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda: "In this context, *brahmavidyā* is that which is denoted by the word *upaniṣad*, because for those intent upon it, there is the absolute cessation of transmigratory existence along with its cause."
Because the root *sad* preceded by the prefix *upa-ni* has that specific meaning [of "sitting down near"], the text itself is called an *upaniṣad* due to its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*).

And that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is of eight kinds: perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), scripture (*āgama*), comparison (*upamāna*), postulation (*arthāpatti*), non-existence (*abhāva*), probability (*sambhava*), and tradition (*aitihya*).
[Page 002] Examination of Direct Perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In this regard, direct perception is correct, non-mediated experience.
That [perception] is of two kinds: conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
Among these, conceptual perception has as its object an entity qualified by a name and so forth, such as "this is a jar."
Non-conceptual [perception] has as its object a thing not delineated by words;
it is the experience of the mere thing, such as "this.
Furthermore, that is of two kinds: the direct perception of yogis and the direct perception of non-yogis.
In this context, non-yogic perception has as its object a thing in contact with the sense faculties.
The sense faculties are of two kinds, distinguished as external and internal.
The five external ones are the cognitive faculties known as hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell.
The internal [factors] are those called mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*).
Objects (*artha*) are of two kinds, distinguished as external and internal.
The external ones are sound and so forth, as well as space and so forth.
Internal [objects] are pleasure and so forth, as well as cognition and so forth.

The contact between sense faculty and object, however, is fivefold: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence (*samavāya*), and inherence in the inherent (*samavetasamavāya*).
There is also a sixth relation characterized by identity (*tādātmya*).
Thus, this [consciousness] is established in the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*).
Nor is there any impossibility of identity between those two— the insentient and the sentient—
since such identity is possible according to the analogy of wood and fire.
Furthermore, the difficulty of that connection being of the nature of *māyā* is actually an ornament [to the system].
Consequently, the cognition "I am this" arises;
therein, the non-objective aspect (*anidamaṃśa*), which is the Self, shines forth by its own nature.
Because consciousness has a single flavor;
the objective aspect (idamaṃśa) appears as a mixture with the intellect and self-consciousness, because it is of the nature of the non-intelligent.
Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that neither the self nor the intellect shines forth in the form of "I," because the self,

being self-luminous, cannot be the object of the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya), and because the self continues to manifest even during deep sleep, fainting, death, and so forth, despite the absence of the "I-notion."
Nor is it logical that consciousness alone appears [in this way],
because, being insentient (jaḍa), it cannot be established as appearing without its own fusion with the self.
Therefore, it must be accepted that both consciousness and the self appear through their mutual identity in the form "I."
Because pleasure and other qualities are inherent in a cognition that possesses identity with the self, they are apprehended as "I am happy" and so forth.
The perception of substances such as a jar occurs through the contact of the eye with a cognition permeated by the light of the self.
Likewise, the perception of color and other qualities residing in those substances occurs through inherence in that which is conjoined with the eye in such a manner.

Just as in the case of [the cognition], "This jar is large and white," there is the apprehension of universals such as "jar-ness" and "whiteness" residing in the color and so forth of the jar, due to inherence-in-that-which-is-inherently-connected-with-the-eye (cakṣuḥsaṃyuktasamavetasamavāya).
The apprehension of sound occurs through its inherence in an auditory organ that possesses an intellect non-different from the self;

likewise, the apprehension of universals such as "sound-ness" occurs through its inherence in that which inheres in such an auditory organ, as for example: "This mountain cave is resonant with sound."
In this way, the cognition of form occurs through the eye alone;
the cognition of sound through the ear alone;
and the cognition of touch through the skin alone.
The cognition of taste occurs through the sense of taste alone;
the cognition of smell occurs through the sense of smell alone;
and the cognition of pleasure and so forth occurs through the internal organ alone.
And that form of the mind (manas) is the means for establishing the mere appearance of an object;
the form of cognition (buddhi) is the means for its ascertainment;
and the form of the ego (ahaṅkāra) is the cause for its superimposition upon the self.
The means for investigating the nature of the mind is as follows:
"This is a pot; this is indeed a pot."
When there is the apprehension of form by the eye alone, such as "I know the jar" or "the jar is known by me," [it is so].
By that same [means], the substance which is the substratum of that [quality] is also apprehended;
the same applies to other cases as well.
However, the ether (*vyoman*), which is the substratum of sound, is apprehended by the mind alone.
The apprehension of the inherence of various substances and qualities occurs through their relationship as qualifier and qualified with the sense organs and their respective connections;
for example, "the inherence of color in the jar" or "the jar possesses the inherence of color."
The direct knowledge of the reality of both the manifest world and the unmanifest is the perception of the yogi.

In that state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), by means of the eye of the mind alone— whose cataracts have been purified through the power of the yoga of devotion and knowledge practiced for a long time and without interruption— one grasps the extraordinary reality of the Self itself, namely, "I am Brahman."

In the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), there is the apprehension of the reality of the world and the non-world—consisting of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the cause of enjoyment—by means of the eye of scripture accompanied by a mind refined through yoga.
The Definition of Inference:
Inference is the correct experience of something imperceptible through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
For example, the knowledge of the pervader, such as fire, by means of the pervaded, such as smoke.
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the probans with the probandum by virtue of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvataḥ*).
It is of two kinds,
distinguished as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
In this context, *anvaya* (positive concomitance) is the pervasion of the general probans by the general probandum, as in:

"Wherever there is smoke, there is fire. *Vyatireka* (negative concomitance) is the pervasion of the absence of the general probandum by the absence of the general probans, as in: "Wherever fire is absent, there smoke is also absent."
The term "correctly" (*samyak*) is used to exclude inference [based on fallacious signs], such as inferring fire from steam or vapor.
The term "indirect" (*parokṣa*) is used to exclude perception (*pratyakṣa*). The term "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*) is used to exclude scriptural testimony (*āgama*).

And that is of two kinds: inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) and inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). That which does not depend on the instruction of another is for oneself; that which depends upon it is for others.
Instruction for others, however, consists of a statement with three members;
the members are either the proposition, the reason, and the example, or the example, the application, and the conclusion.
In that context, the statement of the subject as possessing the property to be proven is the thesis (*pratijñā*).
For example: "This mountain possesses fire.
The statement of the mark (*liṅga*) is the reason (*hetu*);
for example: "Because it possesses smoke."
An example is a statement of correct observation:
"Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just as a kitchen hearth";
or alternatively, "Whatever does not possess fire does not possess smoke either, just as a body of water."

Is the application (*upanaya*) the statement of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of a comparison with the example, wherein the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) have an established inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) in the example;
for instance, "and this [subject] possesses smoke," or "but this [subject] does not possess smoke"? No.
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition together with its reason;
for example, "therefore it possesses fire," or "therefore it does not possess fire," or "it is not so."

That [reason], moreover, is of three kinds, based on the distinction between positive-and-negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*), pure positive concomitance (*kevalānvayin*), and pure negative concomitance (*kevalavyatirekin*).
Among these, the positive-and-negative concomitant reason possesses five characteristics.
The characteristics, however, are: presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), existence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattva*), and exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛtti*).
[The requirements are] that the object [of the reason] is not sublated and that there is no counter-argument.

The subject (dharmin) qualified by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is the thesis (pakṣa). In that context, the presence of the reason (hetu) as a pervading occurrence within it is "property-of-the-subject" (pakṣadharmatva).

The subject (dharmin) possessing a property similar to that which is to be proven (sādhya) is the similar instance (sapakṣa). Existence [of the reason] in all or some part of that is "presence in the similar instance" (sapakṣe sattvam).
The subject possessing a property dissimilar to that which is to be proven is the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
In that regard, the non-occurrence of the reason in every [instance] of the counter-example (vipakṣa) is its exclusion from the counter-example.

The occurrence of the reason in the proposed object of proof (pratijñāta-artha) which is not contradicted by valid cognition (pramāṇa) is the state of having an uncontradicted objective domain (abādhitaviṣayatva).
The absence of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is the state of having no counter-argument (asatpratipakṣatva).

Inferential reasoning based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekyanumāna*), however, possesses both positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*) and negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) between the probans (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*); thus, it is said to have five characteristics (*pañcarūpa*).
For example: "The subject of dispute is false, because it is perceptible."
Whatever is perceived is false, just like a city of the Gandharvas and so forth;
and wherever there is falsity, there is something perceived, as in the case of the self.

The purely positive (kevalānvayi) [reason] possesses four characteristics; for, since there is no absence from the counter-example due to the non-existence of a counter-example, its status as purely positive would not be established if such a counter-example were present.
For example: "The subject of dispute possesses an agent, because it is an effect;
whatever is an effect possesses an agent, as for instance a jar.
The purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) also possesses four characteristics.
Because there is no similar instance (sapakṣa) present, there is an absence of existence in the similar class.
For example: "Every effect is preceded by an omniscient creator, because it is an effect;
whatever is not preceded by an omniscient creator is not an effect, as in the case of the self."
In these inferences, the defects of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*udāharaṇa*) must be avoided.

The defects of the proposition are: having a meaning already established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), having a meaning sublated by that [other means], having a redundant qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*), and having a redundant qualificand (*vyarthaviśeṣyatva*). For example: "Fire is a burner," "Fire is not hot," "This mountain possesses reddish fire," and "The world under dispute is false."
[The faults of] being unestablished (*asiddhatva*), contradictory (*viruddhatva*), or deficient (*hīnatva*) [are thus avoided].

Thus, inference capable of instructing another consists of three members—either those beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*) and ending with the example (*udāharaṇa*), or those beginning with that [example] and ending with the conclusion (*nigamana*).
And it is established that this [inference] is divided into three types according to the different kinds of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The definition of verbal testimony (*āgama*). Verbal testimony is the correct experience of an object not in contact [with the senses] arising from the cognition of a word.
The term "not in contact" is stated for the purpose of excluding perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The term "correctly" (*samyak*) is for the purpose of excluding knowledge derived from the speech of a deceiver;
the phrase "from the cognition of words" (*śabdavijñānāt*) is for the purpose of excluding inference (*anumāna*).
The word "object" (*artha*) is used to exclude [cognitions] such as "drink poison" or "eat space.
As they have said:
"That which is produced by the cognition of a word, which is well-ascertained regarding an object not present [to the senses],"
For the wise declare that valid cognition consists solely of direct perception and inference.

Thus, that scripture (āgama) is of two kinds, distinguished as being of human origin (pauruṣeya) and not of human origin (apauruṣeya). The Veda, which is not of human origin, is fourfold, distinguished as Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan.
And their six limbs consist of the divisions of phonetics (śikṣā), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), prosody (chandas), astronomy (jyotiḥ), and ritual (kalpa).
Human-authored [scripture] is threefold, distinguished by the fifth Veda, the Upavedas, and the Smṛtis.
Among these, the fifth Veda is twofold, through the distinction between Itihāsa and Purāṇa.
Itihāsa consists of the Mahābhārata;
the Purāṇas are of eighteen kinds. And so it is said in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
“This ancient [Purāṇa] is taught as tenfold and eightfold:
the Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata.”
The Bhaviṣya, the Nāradīya, and after that the Mārkaṇḍeya; the Āgneya, the Brahmavaivarta, the Laiṅga, and the Vārāha as well.
The Skānda, the Vāmana, the Kaurma, the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa,
and the Brahmāṇḍa— this is the meritorious sequence of the Purāṇas.”
Thus,

the Upavedas are of four kinds, distinguished as the Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Arthaveda, and Gāndharvaveda. The Smṛtis are the treatises on the duties of the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma) composed by Manu and others.
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas,
Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati.
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama,
Śātātapa, and Vasiṣṭha are the promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras.

Furthermore, the fourfold Veda, characterized by the Ṛgveda and the others, is each twofold— consisting of the Pūrva-kāṇḍa and the Uttara-kāṇḍa— due to the distinction between the subjects of Dharma and Brahman.
The same applies to the fifth Veda as well.
Because it is of the nature of an exposition of that [work].
As it is said in the Vāyavīya:
"The twice-born who may know the four Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs and the Upaniṣads..."
If he did not know the ancient [teachings], he would certainly not be wise.
"One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He will deceive me.'"
Thus,
in that regard, although *dharma*— which has the formative nature (*saṃskāra*) of virtuous action— is devoid of self,
it is nonetheless not in contact [with the senses] because it cannot be apprehended by the eye or other faculties due to its lack of material form (*rūpa*).
It is an "object" (artha) because it is the cause of both worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
Since Brahman is the Self, it cannot be grasped by the senses as their presiding witness; thus, it is "not in contact" (asannikṛṣṭa).
However, because its nature is bliss, it is an "object"—this is the distinction.
Furthermore, because these two [phenomena] have a nature that is beyond direct perception (*parokṣa-svabhāva*), knowledge of them is indirect;
whereas, because Brahman is characterized as the reality of the self that is eternally non-indirect (*nityāparokṣātmatattva-lakṣaṇa*), knowledge of it is direct.
Otherwise, both types of knowledge would result in being non-conformable with reality (*ayathārtha*).

In that regard, according to the maxim "the established is taught for the sake of what is to be accomplished," the knowledge of *dharma* is the correct experience of an object not [otherwise] proximate, arising from the word in the form of an injunction (*vidhi*) which has the mantra as its meaning.

According to the maxim "what is to be accomplished is taught for the sake of the established," the knowledge of *brahman* is the correct experience of an object not [otherwise] proximate, arising from the collection of scriptural passages (*śruti*) consisting of injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras, which take the form of great sentences (*mahāvākya*).
Dharma is divided into two types by virtue of being the means for attaining what is desired and avoiding what is undesired.
Among these, the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other such rites are the means for attaining desired ends such as heaven.
The meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is characterized by the rule of non-violence toward all beings and serves as the means for avoiding what is undesirable;

consequently, the meaning of injunctions and prohibitions (*niṣedha*) is that which is a means for attaining the desirable and avoiding the undesirable—provided it is fit for human action—and not merely "that which is to be done" (*kāryamātra*).
For if it were merely that, people acting with deliberation would not engage in an injunction such as "Eat poison."
Nor is it a means for attaining the desired or avoiding the undesired,
because there is no inclination toward action from such a sentence as "The moon has risen.
Child, drink from the breast!
This same principle applies even to ordinary worldly sentences such as "Do not touch the fire.
Thus, the apprehension of the power of words also refers only to what is a beneficial means suitable for action (*kṛti-yogya*), and not to the "task" (*kārya*) itself.
For example, in the sentence "Bring the cow," the apprehension of that [word-meaning] occurs only with respect to a beneficial means.

Just as in the statement "a son has been born to you," there is the apprehension of that [fact]; therefore, since Brahman is established, one should not dispute the authority of the Vedāntas. Furthermore, injunctive sentences are of two kinds, according to whether their fruit is visible or invisible.
In that regard, in the earlier section (pūrvakāṇḍa), rites such as the Kārīrī sacrifice have perceptible results;
in the later section (uttarakāṇḍa), the injunctions prescribing hearing [the Upanishads] and so forth for the sake of realizing the Self have perceptible results.
Since their authority is thus demonstrated, the authority of other [Vedic texts] may be inferred by the mark (liṅga) of their being Veda.
Brahman is twofold, distinguished by its having attributes (*saguṇa*) and its being devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*).
The qualified (*saguṇa*) Brahman is further twofold, distinguished by the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).
Among these, that which is taught in the Vedas as characterized by existence, consciousness, infinity, and so forth, is the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman.
The Lord with attributes (saguṇa-aiśvara) is taught in the form of being the cause of the world and so forth;
the individual soul (jīva-rūpa) is taught in the form of entering the phenomenal world (prapañca) created by Himself and so forth.

These great sentences (mahāvākyas), such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), aided by those [scriptural passages] dedicated to the purification of the categories of reality (tattva-padārtha), teach the identity of Brahman and the Self—a supreme human goal not known through any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, it is precisely those [Vedas] that teach the attainment of the supreme human goal through the understanding of that [reality].

Thus, because the Veda— divided into the nature of the earlier and later sections (*pūrvottara-kāṇḍa*)— is embraced by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) and its intended meaning has been ascertained, the Mīmāṃsā treatise was composed for the purpose of investigating that meaning.
And that [work] consists of three sections (kāṇḍas) comprising twenty chapters.
Among these, the Pūrvamīmāṃsā, consisting of twelve chapters, is devoted to the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa);
its author is Jaimini.
The author of the Bhāṣya is Śabarasvāmin;
his two commentators are Bhaṭṭa Kumārila and Prabhākara.
Of these two, by Bhaṭṭa Kumārila, injunctive sentences were explained as being centered on *bhāvanā*.
Prabhākara [interprets it] as being focused on *niyoga*.

However, the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*—composed by Vyāsa in eight chapters—is of two kinds, being grounded in both the qualified (*saguṇa*) and unqualified (*nirguṇa*) Brahman. Among these, that which is grounded in the qualified Brahman consists of four chapters comprising the section on the deities (*devatākāṇḍa*).
Here, the author of the Bhāṣya is Saṅkarṣa.

In that work, it is established in the first chapter that the purpose of all the remaining portions of the mantras is to convey the true nature of the deities. In the second [chapter], it is demonstrated that the remainder of the Veda—consisting of injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), and so forth—is subordinate to the mantras and the deities.
In the third [chapter], it was shown that the reality of the deity (*devatātattva*) is adorned with a multitude of qualities, such as having a form according to one's own will (*svecchāvigraha*).

In the fourth, the fruit of the worship of the deity was determined to consist in the attainment of the splendor, sovereignty, and bliss of various worlds through the grace of those respective deities, manifested in their particular attire and ornaments.
Thus, the *Madhyamīmāṃsā* establishes Hari as the self of all deities and is therefore devoted to the Brahman-with-attributes (*saguṇabrahman*).
The section consisting of knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa), however, is the culmination in the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇabrahmaniṣṭhā);
it also comprises four chapters.
Its commentator is Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda.

Furthermore, certain partial adherents (ekadeśins) such as Brahmadatta, Bhāskara, Rāmānuja, Ānandatīrtha, and others, composed spurious commentaries on that [Brahma-sūtra] due to their differing views.
Here, by means of the first chapter, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all Vedānta texts with Brahman, the innermost reality (*pratyaktattva*), has been demonstrated.
By the second [chapter], contradictions with other means of valid cognition such as perception are refuted;
by the third, the internal means for the knowledge of Brahman—namely hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption—are taught along with their foundations;
and by the fourth chapter, the fruit of knowledge characterized as immediate or gradual liberation, as well as the fruit of meditation, are described.
And liberation is precisely the cessation of the ignorance regarding the Self (*ātman-vidyā*).
Therefore, the *Karmakāṇḍa* was composed for the sake of the ignorant person who, setting aside the inquiry into the Self, seeks only the means for attaining pleasure and avoiding pain;
and the *Devatākāṇḍa* was composed for one who desires the happiness of residing in the same world (*sālokya*) as the deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, Soma, Sūrya, Anila, and Anala.

The Brahmakāṇḍa has been set forth with reference to the most excellent of men—one who is detached from all worldly pleasures, who desires only the bliss of liberation from bondage, and who seeks to know the true nature of the Self. Enough of this prolixity;

for the science of logic (Tarkaśāstra) serves as an auxiliary limb (upāṅga) of the Veda, as it is intent upon washing away the mire of doubts regarding its lack of authority—such as those imputed by Buddhists and others based on the grounds of being the words of an unreliable person or containing mutually contradictory meanings—and because it defines the instruments of knowledge (pramāṇa), the objects of knowledge (prameya), the knower (pramātṛ), and so forth, which are required [by the Vedānta].
That [system], however, is twofold, distinguished as Naiyāyika and Vaiśeṣika.
Among these, the Naiyāyika is based on sixteen categories and was originated by Akṣapāda;
the Vaiśeṣika is based on six categories and was originated by Kaṇāda.

As for the Sāṅkhya system, which is twofold— divided into the atheistic (nirīśvara) and the theistic (seśvara)— it is included within the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and therefore it is not counted separately.
Of these two, Kapila composed the atheistic Sāṅkhya, which rests upon twenty-five principles;
Patañjali composed the theistic Sāṅkhya, which rests upon twenty-six principles,
by means of which he provided the commentary (*bhāṣya*) for the grammar consisting of eight chapters (*aṣṭādhyāyī*) composed by Pāṇini.
Thus there are eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
These were bestowed upon Brahmā by the Supreme Person at the beginning of the aeon (*kalpa*).
And so it is stated in the Śrī-Vāyavīya:
“The auxiliary sciences, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā,
the extensive Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.”
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and thereafter Arthaśāstra; these are traditionally recorded as the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyās).
Regarding these eighteen branches of knowledge with their diverse paths,
the sacred tradition (śruti) declares that the poet Śūlapāṇi himself was their original author.
For he, the Lord of the entire world, desiring to create the whole universe,
first directly appointed the eternal Brahmā as his son.
To that first-born son, Brahmā, the source of the universe,
the Lord formerly imparted these sciences for the sake of the world’s maintenance.

Thus, these branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) were set forth in this world by Brahmā through the mouths of Marīci and others; however, because of defects such as short lifespans and diminished intellect among humans in this age, they could not be maintained in their entirety.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord himself, having assumed the form of Vyāsa, condensed them.
As it is said in the second book:
“Alas! For men whose vision is closed by time and whose lifespan is short, their own scripture has a shore far away.”
For he, appearing age after age, shall indeed divide branch by branch the tree of the Vedas within Satyavatī.”
Thus, the means of valid cognition known as scripture (āgama) has been examined. Now follows the examination of other means of valid cognition, such as comparison (upamāna) and the rest.
Now, regarding analogy (*upamāna*):

when a village-dweller has been asked, "What are the characteristics of the animal called a *gavaya*? and receives the answer from another forest-dweller, "A *gavaya* is just like a cow," that person later goes to the forest and, by chance, upon seeing a *gavaya*, [perceives] the similarity between the cow and the *gavaya*.
And when a perceptual recognition arises whose object is similarity— such as "my cow is similar to this"— that is comparison (*upamāna*).
As they have said:
"And when the meaning of a sentence containing unfamiliar words [is understood] with respect to the named object,
that direct perceptual recognition is here called analogy (upamāna)."
Thus:
presumption (*arthāpatti*) is an experience arising from the impossibility of [the perceived fact] being otherwise.
It is of two kinds, distinguished as that which is based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and that which is based on what is heard (*śruta*).
In this regard, the certainty that the observed movement of the sun from one location to another is not possible without actual motion is *dṛṣṭārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is perceived).

The certainty regarding the *apūrva* (unseen potency) in the interim—that the efficacy of a momentary sacrifice to produce a result occurring at a different time and place, as heard in scripture, is not possible without such a refinement—is *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard).
The certainty of non-existence resulting from the non-perception of something despite its perceptibility is the means of knowledge known as *abhāva* (non-apprehension).
Just as in the case of "there is no jar here on this ground," the determination of a supersensible object that arises from the thought "this matter is possible" is *saṃbhava* (presumption).
Just as the determination of the incarnations of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others arises from descriptions such as those concerning the lunar and solar lineages;
and traditional lore (*aitihya*) is the knowledge arising from an oral tradition whose original speaker has not been specified.
For example: "A yakṣa dwells in this banyan tree.
But from where was it determined that there are exactly these many means of valid cognition? "The Cārvākas hold perception to be the only one; Kaṇāda and Sugata [hold two]..."
And they [the Sāṅkhyas] accept inference, as well as that [scriptural testimony], and they also accept verbal testimony.

The followers of the Nyāya school who accept only one part [of its system] likewise [accept three]; some also include analogy; and Prabhākara says that these four, together with presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), [constitute the means of valid cognition].
"The Bhaṭṭas and likewise the Vedāntins hold that these [means of knowledge] have non-existence as the sixth;
the Paurāṇikas, however, have declared them to be joined with probability (sambhava) and tradition (aitihya)."
Thus, according to the statement of those who know the principles of logic.

Through this investigation into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) may also be characterized. The cognizer is the substratum of the act of cognition.
The object of valid cognition is the "knowable" (*prameya*). Here, treatises of inquiry are of two kinds, distinguished as Vedic and non-Vedic;
and each of these is further threefold, according to the divisions of Mīmāṃsā, Sāṅkhya, and Tarka.
This is due to the divisions of the Buddhist, Ārhata, and Lokāyata schools. Among them, the first triad is Vedic because it is rooted in the Vedas;
the latter triad is non-Vedic because it is rooted in counterfeit Vedas composed by the Buddha, the Kṣapaṇaka, and Bṛhaspati.
Thus, there are six philosophical systems.

The Exposition of the Cārvāka Doctrine. In this regard, for the Cārvāka— the founder of the Lokāyata school who maintains that perception alone is the means of valid cognition— the body itself, which is established by direct perception as the locus of the quality of consciousness (caitanya) through such cognitions as "I am a human," "I am fat," and "I am thin," is the knower (pramātṛ).

The objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are the four principles (*tattva*) characterized by earth, water, fire, and air, which, by virtue of arising in various high and low bodily forms, undergo both combination and subsequent dissolution.
The goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) are only wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*), not dharma.
Furthermore, the two Vedas are those established upon these [two goals], namely the Arthaveda and the Gāndharvaveda.

Since there is no dharma, there is likewise no such thing as adharma. Consequently, heaven and hell do not exist as its fruits. Due to their absence, there is no Supreme Lord whatsoever who ordains them for embodied beings.
Death itself is liberation.
The treatises on wealth and pleasure (*arthakāma-śāstra*) and the Lokāyata treatise are included therein because they are rooted in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, an inference such as "this food removes hunger because it is food, like yesterday's food" is also included therein.
Because there is no difference in their having perception as their basis,

it is the established conclusion that the Veda— which concerns dharma and Brahman and has the fruits of worldly prosperity and the supreme good— is indeed not a means of valid knowledge, since its subject matter consists of objects beyond the senses.
And thus says that [author]:
"The Agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and smearing oneself with ashes—
these are merely the livelihood of those devoid of intelligence and manliness," so said Bṛhaspati.
The authors of the Veda are the sages, the buffoons, and the night-stalkers;
for heaven belongs to the sacrificers even when the agent, the action, and the substance have perished.
There might be fruit for trees scorched by a forest fire;
but there can be no fruit for one who propounds a thesis that contradicts objects established by means of valid cognition, such as direct perception.
"If the Vedāntas are indeed scriptures, what offense has been committed by the Buddhists? and so forth.
The Exposition of the Jain Doctrine.

Between the two—the Jain and the Buddhist—who both maintain the authority of perception and inference, this is the established tenet of the Jain: "Because of the experience 'this body is mine,' the body has a seer distinct from itself;

or else, because it is an object of sight and is composed of the elements, like a jar. [This is known] through inference, as well as from the observation that vital breath, movement, consciousness, memory, and so forth are absent in a dead body.

Furthermore, it is not correct to argue that because [the self] is not perceived, one should not accept a cognizer called the "self"— a specific luminous substance distinct from the body, whether equal in dimension to it or of atomic dimension—
as an object beyond the senses, on the grounds that such an admission would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Because it would follow that the validity of perception must be admitted as being beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).
Therefore, by virtue of the authority of the scriptures composed by the Sage Arhat, dharma and adharma, as well as heaven and hell, also exist.

And *dharma* consists of such practices as plucking out the hair, wandering for alms, carrying a peacock feather, celibacy, fasting, going without clothing, bathing with pure water, bowing to the Arhats, and climbing heated stones.
However, rituals such as the Agnihotra are merely semblances of dharma,
because they are accomplished through the injury of moving and non-moving living beings; furthermore,
the lack of authority of the Veda is determined by its being the speech of an unreliable person, by its internal contradictions, and so forth.
Adharma is characterized by harm to living beings and the like.

The bodies of moving and non-moving entities, which possess causes, are composed of earth, water, fire, and air atoms—also known as *pudgala*—which are impelled by the karma of living beings called dharma and adharma; these are objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
Furthermore, the atoms themselves are established through inference.
And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*): The gradation of atomic dimension must terminate somewhere,
because it is a gradation of dimension.
It is like the varying degrees of magnitude in great objects. This world, consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, is characterized by manifoldness (*anekānta*).
Through the knowledge of this, liberation—characterized by the constant upward progression of embodied beings who are devoted to virtues such as non-violence—is accomplished.
As they have said:
"Syādvāda, because it abandons all one-sidedness (ekānta) through the application of the interrogative particle 'kim' and the employment of the suffix 'cit',
and because it relies upon the method of the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī), serves for the knowledge of reality."
Thus,
"indefiniteness" (anaikāntikatva) refers to the state of having an indeterminate form by way of being existent, non-existent, and so forth;
and that is established through the method of the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgīnaya).
How so?
It may exist; it may not exist; it may be inexpressible.
It may both exist and not exist;
it may both exist and be inexpressible; it may both not exist and be inexpressible.
The logic of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnyāya*) consists of: "it may be that it exists," "it may be that it does not exist," and "it may be inexpressible.
The particle *syāt* is an indeclinable used to indicate non-absolutism (*anaikāntikatva*).
When asked whether the world, consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, exists, he replies: "It may be that it exists."
The meaning is that it is not ascertained by way of its own nature, because it possesses birth and so forth.
In the same manner, this should also be understood in cases such as "it might not exist."
Because it is being experienced, there is no certainty of its non-existence.
Because it is denotable by words such as "blue" or "pleasure," there is no certainty of its being undenotable.
Since existence and non-existence are contradictory and thus cannot coexist in a single substratum, there is no certainty of its possessing both natures.
Because it is also appropriate to say "it does not exist," there is the uncertainty that it both exists and is inexpressible;
because it is also fitting to say "it exists," there is the uncertainty that it does not exist and is inexpressible.
Because it is appropriate to say both "it exists" and "it does not exist," there is an uncertainty that it both exists, does not exist, and is inexpressible.

Having thus ascertained the universe to be empty of any fixed state, the person who has attained world-weariness through the power of yoga reaches liberation, characterized by constant upward progression. This concludes the exposition of the Sugata’s doctrine.
Because, if the self were of atomic dimension, it would be impossible for it to simultaneously experience sensations occurring in all its parts;
if it were of the same dimension as the body, external objects could not be known, and there would follow the consequence of its being non-eternal like a jar;
and because if everything were non-conclusive, then non-conclusiveness itself would likewise result in being non-conclusive.

Furthermore, according to the maxim "all elevations end in a fall," since liberation—characterized as a state of perpetual upward movement—would itself end in a fall, its status as an eternal human goal (nitya-puruṣārtha) is not established; thus, this position is not free from defects. Therefore, the system of the Sugata is now undertaken.
This very system is divided into four types according to the differences among its disciples.

And the disciples—the Mādhyamikas, Yogācāras, Sautrāntikas, and Vaibhāṣikas—possess degrees of purity according to their respective order. Among them, for the Mādhyamika, who is the most excellent candidate, the cognizer has emptiness as its intrinsic nature;
this is because one who has awakened from sleep observes a memory such as, "I was empty for all this time."
Furthermore, the appearance of a "being" (sattva) within the self, such as the thought "I am," has for its object conventional reality (saṃvṛtti-tattva).
The same applies to cognitions such as "the jar exists.
Therefore, even the object of cognition (prameya) is indeed empty.
Because the destruction of that which exists is impossible;
likewise, even valid cognition is in reality empty,
because birth and destruction are untenable for that which exists.
The cognition of existence is merely conventional (saṃvṛtti).

What is called "convention" is a thing whose specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is inexpressible in terms of categories such as existence and non-existence, and which is the cause for the appearance of what is non-existent as existent.

Therefore, the established conclusion is as follows: since the triad beginning with the subject (*pramātṛ*) is in reality non-existent yet appears as having the nature of existence, for the practitioner who serves the Sugata-Muni— the teacher of that [truth]— who is attended by the five Buddhas, with body, speech, and mind, and who has for a long time and continuously meditated upon "all is empty," when the [notion of] emptiness itself has dissolved within his mind, liberation, characterized by the attainment of the emptiness of all things, will be accomplished.

However, for the Yogācāra who stands on this side [of that], since there is no cognizer (*pramātṛ*), there can be no establishment of the object of cognition (*prameya*) as emptiness; therefore, some cognizer must be admitted.
And he is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), otherwise it would follow that another means of proof would be required.
Furthermore, self-luminosity is not possible for anything other than consciousness; therefore,

having established through perception that "I am," and through inference that the body is not the Self because it is an object of sight— just like a pot— the ālayavijñāna, which perishes and arises moment by moment, is the knower.
It is precisely because of the stability of the continuum that there arises the conceit of stability within it.
The thought, "I who saw an elephant this morning am now seeing a mass of darkness and remember it"—this is merely a non-delusion, like [the illusion of] a flame.

The five aggregates known as form (*rūpa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) arise and dissolve moment by moment according to the karma of living beings; by their very nature, they undergo transformation and cessation in the forms of gods, humans, and denizens of hell.
And these constitute the objects of cognition (*prameya*).
Among them, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of the sense faculties and their respective objects;
the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the cognition thereof.
The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, which are the fruits of that [contact].
The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) consists of perceptions distinguished by qualities, actions, and genus;
for example, here [the perceptions] "cow," "horse," or "man."
The universal (*jāti*) consists of such things as "cowness," "horseness," and "humanity.
The quality (*guṇa*) consists of such things as "white," "red," and "black."

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is characterized by momentum (*vega*), contraction (*veṣṭana*), elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*), and so forth; momentum is that which belongs to rabbits and the like. Actions such as standing, walking, and sitting, as well as specific cognitions such as "it has horns," "it has four feet," and "it has a tail," [arise from it].
Wrapping refers to that of birch bark and the like; elasticity refers to that of branches and the like;
and the object of cognition is that which possesses the characteristics previously described.
If that [object] were distinct from the manifestation, it would not manifest at all; therefore, everything is nothing but the form of cognition.
If cognition were stable, then blue, yellow, and so forth would appear to everyone at all times.
"Never for anyone"—thus it is indeed unstable.
Therefore, this entire world, consisting of the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping, is eternally submerged within the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna* under the notion of "I.

Consequently, for that person who is devoted to the true Dharma—such as venerating caityas and practicing the path toward the Buddhas—and who has long cultivated the realization that "all this is merely consciousness," liberation arises right here in this very life, consisting of the emergence of a purified continuum of consciousness.
This is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Therefore, for a later disciple named Sautrāntika, because everything would reside within [the mind], it would be non-existent externally; consequently, it would be impossible for it to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and there would follow the undesirable consequence of contradiction with both error and sublation.

Furthermore, if cognition were to possess the form of the object of knowledge, it would follow that it is insentient; therefore, their distinctness must be accepted. Thus, the entire universe—both external and internal—truly exists.

And if that [universe] were permanent, the various successive states observed in a seed—such as its swelling, becoming a sprout, a tree, putting forth leaves, flowering, and bearing fruit—could not be accounted for.
Consequently, one must accept that it consists of momentary particularities (*kṣaṇika-svalakṣaṇa*).
If the knower were thus stable, then because cognition would also be stable, one would always perceive blue and never yellow,
or anything contrary to it.
Therefore, even the knower is indeed unstable.
This much is the distinction: internal cognition, being a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*);
external [objects] such as blue and so forth are merely inferable (*anumeya*).
For example: the reflection of the object of knowledge in consciousness is preceded by the original object,
because it is a reflection.
It is like the reflection of a face in a mirror.
And thus, there is no external object graspable by direct perception. For even the Vaibhāṣika, who is the most recent of disciples, holds that the external object exists and is directly perceived.
Because this [object] appears as "this is blue" precisely through direct perception,
there is only this much difference between these two;
everything else is identical.

And among these positions, since the scriptures concerning the Buddha and so forth are rooted in inference, they are included within that very category; thus, there is no increase in the number of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

In that regard, when the Sautrāntikas and Vaibhāṣikas have understood through the scripture that "everything is momentary" and, while serving the Teacher, the Blessed Tathāgata, and his devotees, the direct realization of the momentariness of all things has arisen, [they attain] the state consisting in the acquisition of a purified continuum of consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna-santānatā*).
The established doctrine is that one attains liberation.
Ultimately, all three of these are proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*).
How so?
The Yogācāra proclaims the emptiness of external objects;
the Sautrāntika [proclaims] the emptiness of external objects that are directly perceived;
and the Vaibhāṣika declares the emptiness of the unstable world, both external and internal.

Here is a summary: "The primary Mādhyamika considers the entire world to be a transformation (*vivarta*) of emptiness; for in the Yogācāra view, cognitions exist, and the entire object is their transformation; the Sautrāntika infers through cognition that objects exist as momentary; and the Vaibhāṣika declares that everything is directly perceived and momentary."
Thus [it is said].

Herein, because there would be the consequence of non-establishment due to the absence of a proof for the world having emptiness as its intrinsic nature, [the following is stated].
Furthermore, it contradicts the experience of sentient beings;
for if cognition were to possess the form of the object, it would follow that it is insentient,
and it would follow that the object is not perceived externally.
If that which appears directly as "this," namely blue, were inferable, then it would follow that even the specific characteristic of cognition appearing as "I" must be considered inferable;
furthermore, if the cognizer were unstable, it would be impossible for memory—which pertains to an object previously experienced—to occur;
and if the object of cognition were momentary, recognition in the form "this is that very same jar" would be impossible.

Although cognitions of objects such as blue, which consist of modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), are subject to appearance and disappearance, it is established that the consciousness which is the witness of the intellect (*buddhi-sākṣi-caitanya*) is stable.

Since there is no differentiator for knowledge devoid of objective coloring (*viṣayoparāga*), and because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it is impossible to ascertain its birth or destruction either intrinsically or extrinsically;

furthermore, since an unknown object cannot be denied existence, the position of the Sugata (Buddha) must be disregarded, just like the position of the Kṣapaṇakas (Jainas), because—even though he asserts the authority of the Vedas—he accepts their nature as being inferential (*anumānātmatva*).

The doctrine of Kaṇāda, who is included among those who maintain that perception and inference alone are the means of valid cognition, is introduced here: "In this system, there are exactly six categories (padārtha): substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence."
In that context, substance possesses qualities;
it is divided into nine kinds,
through the distinctions of earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind.
Among these, the eighth substance, called the Self (*ātman*), is the knower (*pramātṛ*).

It is distinct from the body and other things characterized by earth and so forth; it is eternal, all-pervading, different in each field (*kṣetra*), dependent upon the Supreme Lord, insentient by nature, and apprehended through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*).
The other substances, as well as qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, are the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

A quality (*guṇa*) is that which possesses generality (*sāmānya*), is not an inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and is non-active by nature (*aspandātman*).
