It is divided into twenty-four types based on the distinctions of remoteness (*paratva*), proximity (*aparatva*), heaviness (*gurutva*), fluidity (*dravatva*), viscidity (*snehatva*), cognition (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and sound (*śabda*). Among these, color (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), odor (*gandha*), touch (*sparśa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), remoteness (*paratva*), proximity (*aparatva*), heaviness (*gurutva*), and occasional fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*)— along with mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)— are the qualities of earth (*pṛthivī*).
Water possesses the quality of moisture, excluding odor, and is endowed with the aforementioned qualities [of earth].
The qualities of fire are color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and occasional fluidity, as well as momentum.
The qualities of air are touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and the momentum of velocity.
Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, and sound are the qualities of space.
Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction are the qualities of time.
And these are the qualities of space (*dik*):

number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*) are the qualities of the self (*ātman*).
Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, velocity, and mental impression are the qualities of the mind (*manas*).
The nine specific qualities of the self are cognition and the rest. Sound is the specific quality of space;
touch is that of air.
Form is the quality of fire;
taste is the quality of water;
smell is the quality of earth.

The specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) do not exist in space, time, or the internal organ (*manas*). Action (*karman*), which belongs to the same class as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of conjunction and disjunction,
is of five kinds, distinguished as upward throwing, downward throwing, contraction, expansion, and locomotion.
A universal is eternal and subsists in many [individuals].
It is of two kinds: the higher and the lower.
The higher is existence (*sattā*).
Because it has a wider extension;
the other, such as substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth,
because it has a narrower extension.
The ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣas*) are eternal substrates that serve as the causes for the cognition of absolute distinction; they are infinite in number.
Inherence (*samavāya*) is an eternal relation.
The four elements beginning with earth are both eternal and non-eternal;
however, the five beginning with space are exclusively eternal.

Eternal atoms—divided into those of earth, water, fire, and air—by the will of the Supreme Lord, initiate through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, the entire universe, from bodies and jars up to their ultimate constituent wholes (*avayavin*).
There are four aims of human life, beginning with *dharma*:
*dharma* is characterized by the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth, as well as the propitiation of the Lord (*īśvara*) and the like;
*artha* and *kāma* are those which are not in conflict with *dharma*.

For a person who knows the reality of the six categories, liberation—characterized by the destruction of the nine qualities—occurs through the grace of the Supreme Lord. By him, the aforementioned meaning was realized; and he, the Supreme Lord, possessing the powers of eternal will, knowledge, and action, having created the universe consisting of words and meanings, established the convention of the power of words, such that "this is the meaning of this word."

Since it was composed for the purpose of the worldly prosperity and ultimate liberation of living beings, it is free from the stain of doubt due to its being the speech of the supreme authoritative person (paramāpta).
Furthermore, the existence of the Lord (Īśvara) is ascertained through inference:
the disputed effects, such as the mountains and so forth, possess an agent because they are effects.
Whatever is thus is so, just like a jar and so forth.
This jar is produced by a cognition other than the non-eternal cognition that produces this jar, because it possesses the nature of a jar (*ghaṭatva*).
Based on the inference "like that within a jar," divine knowledge is also inferable.

Nor is it logical to claim that every effect arises from its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) alone; for if one takes the word *svabhāva*—meaning "one's own being" (*svo bhāvaḥ*)—to refer to a non-existent entity, it would entail the absurdity of something arising from itself.
Because it would follow that an effect could arise without a cause when grasping another object related to it;

and because, if the production of the effect were intended to occur without depending on anything else, it would follow that those seeking a jar or similar object would find the taking up of clay and so forth to be useless.
Therefore, because an effect necessarily has a cause,
and since the world is determined to be an effect by virtue of its possessing parts, its cause must be inferred.
A cause is that which exists invariably prior [to the effect].
That [cause] is threefold, due to the distinction between inherent, non-inherent, and instrumental causes. That in which an effect inheres is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*),
such as clay for a jar.
The non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is that which is proximate to the inherent cause (*samavāyin*) and whose causal capacity has been ascertained;
for example, the mutual conjunction of the parts of clay.
The efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) is other than both the inherent and non-inherent causes, and its causal capacity has been ascertained.
Just as in the case of a potter’s staff, wheel, and so forth;
therein, in the production of the world, atoms are the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa),
and their mutual conjunction is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa).
God is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
And birth is the connection with existence (*sattā*) of that which previously did not exist.
Since the created universe consists of pleasure and pain, the karma of living beings also possesses causality here; such is the general direction of the argument.

Scriptural passages such as "From whom indeed... and similar Smṛti texts such as "I am the beginning," as well as those beginning with "His supreme power," are likewise inferential in nature, consisting of the inference of eternal will, knowledge, and effort.
The same principle applies to other Śrutis as well.
Scriptural statements such as "By means of the Jyotiṣṭoma" are of the nature of inference.
For by those [scriptures], the fact that the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites—which are acts of propitiating the Supreme Lord—are the means for achieving results such as heaven is revealed.

In this regard, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: the rites under dispute, such as sacrifices, are the means for achieving the desired result, because they consist in the service of the Lord.
It is like attending upon a worldly lord.
In the same way, even those scriptural passages that enjoin hearing and so forth for the sake of realizing the Self [function similarly].
For they reveal that hearing and so forth regarding the Supreme Self are the means for liberation—characterized by the eradication of all suffering—by way of generating His grace.
In this regard, the formal argument is as follows: the realization of the supreme self is the remover of bondage,
because it is a realization of the self.
"As in our own waking awareness.
Knowledge of the Supreme Self is produced by hearing [the scriptures] and so forth,
because it is knowledge derived from a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And as for the phrase "like the knowledge of dharma":
in Vedic passages such as "O Earth," the very nature of the Supreme Self is stated to be untouched by suffering; thus, liberation is simply the total eradication of suffering.

And since that [eradication] is not possible if other qualities such as intellect (buddhi) still exist, the teacher Kaṇāda records that liberation is characterized by the destruction of the nine qualities.
An Exposition of the System of Akṣapāda:

Regarding Akṣapāda, who maintains that perception, inference, verbal testimony, and comparison are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is the postulation of a cognizer (*pramātṛ*) as in the case of Kaṇāda,
as well as the postulation of the Supreme Lord as a cognizer distinct from [the individual].
The postulation that cognizers possess qualities such as plurality, eternity, omnipresence, and knowledge;
the postulation of their insentience; and the postulation that they are objects known through the notion of "I."
The conceptualization of a perceiver,
the conceptualizations of permanence and impermanence regarding objects of cognition, and the conceptualization that atoms are the originators of the world.
The conceptualization of the triad beginning with dharma,
the conceptualization of bondage and liberation,
and the conceptualization that darkness is not a distinct substance because it is merely the absence of light.
This much is the distinction: Akṣapāda is without distinction [in his approach], being a proponent of sixteen categories (*ṣoḍaśapadārtha*).

Thus says his sūtra: "The attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of the truth (*tattva-jñāna*) regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), tenet (*siddhānta*), members of a syllogism (*avayava*), reasoning (*tarka*), ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), discussion (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)."
From the knowledge of the reality of the sixteen categories comes the cessation of false cognitions, such as the delusion of selfhood regarding the body and other things that are not the self;
from that follows the cessation of defects such as attachment and so forth.

From that follows the cessation of auspicious and inauspicious karma; from that, due to the absence of causes, follows the cessation of birth in various wombs as an effect thereof; and from that follows the cessation of suffering beginning with dwelling in the womb and ending with death—thus, in this sequence, occurs liberation.

And thus states the Sūtra of Akṣapāda: "Upon the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the non-existence of each preceding one, which constitutes liberation (apavarga).

For those followers of the Nyāya school who accept perception, inference, and scripture as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the definition and status of the means of valid cognition and so forth remain exactly as Akṣapāda taught them.
However, for them, liberation is not merely the cessation of suffering.
Moreover, there is also the manifestation of eternal bliss;
even though it is something produced,
its imperishability is established because its nature consists in the total destruction of all suffering.
An exposition of the Sāṃkhya systems, both with and without a Lord:
in all three of these positions, since the self is insentient, its being a knower is untenable;
furthermore, by being the substratum of qualities such as intellect (*buddhi*), it would incur the state of being subject to modification.
Because the Supreme Lord would necessarily be insentient if he were distinct from consciousness;
because the difference between consciousness [and the self] cannot be apprehended either intrinsically or extrinsically;
and because if the self were known through the notion of "I," its insentience could not be avoided, just as in the case of a jar.

Furthermore, if cognitions were to be known by a subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya-jñāna*), then if that [reflective cognition] were admitted to be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets;
if it were luminous by another, it would result in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*);
and if it were an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), its status as a cognition (*jñānatva*) would be untenable.
Because if the Veda were of human origin, it would entail the necessity of depending upon a foundational source of authority;
because if God possessed eternal will and so forth, it would entail the consequence that He possesses an eternal body;
and because if liberation consisted in the destruction of the nine qualities, there would be the defect of its resulting in a state equivalent to that of stones and the like.
If pleasure were merely the absence of pain, then it would not be established that consciousness is the locus of nine qualities;
furthermore, one could equally claim that pain is the absence of pleasure.
[page 028]
Since atoms, being partless, cannot account for grossness even when in mutual conjunction,
and since they would lose their status as atoms if they possessed parts;
and because scriptural passages such as "Know Māyā to be Prakṛti" declare that Māyā alone is the cause of the world.

Because the theory of atoms as the cause [of the world] contradicts the Śruti, it is merely pleasing when left unexamined; thus, the Sāṃkhya position is introduced. Although both the follower of the Nyāya school and the Sāṃkhya advocate perception, inference, and scripture as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, like Akṣapāda, the followers of that [Nyāya] school also maintain that the Veda possesses authority because it was composed by a reliable person (*āpta*). Furthermore, they hold that the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
Because its ascertainment depends on the absence of sublation,
lest even erroneous cognitions be granted the status of valid knowledge;
for the Sāṃkhya, however, all cognitions are in accordance with reality.

By means of the inference, "Because it possesses the nature of being a cognition, like that which is commonly accepted," the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge is established as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*) for one who does not admit cognitions such as error or doubt— just like the Prabhākara—
who considers the universe to be devoid of a Lord (*nirīśvara*).
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like space," and so forth—by such inferences; and [from scripture]:
"The Nāciketa narrative, proclaimed by Death, is eternal;
speech, without beginning or end, was emitted eternally by the Self-existent One."
By such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*), the eternity of the Veda is established equally [for both schools], as in the case of Bhaṭṭa and Kumārila.

Furthermore, cognitions are not merely of the nature of perception (*grahaṇa*) and recollection (*smaraṇa*); for if one does not admit the existence of erroneous (*bhrānti*) and doubtful (*saṃśaya*) cognitions, there would be no account for the cognitions of the body and so forth as being the self, nor for the cognitions of religious duties (*dharma*) such as the worship of deities.

Furthermore, it would follow that [the cognition] would possess the status of valid knowledge (*pramātva*); and since the method of reasoning (*nyāya*) proceeds only when the subject (*dharmin*) is doubted, the absence of doubt would entail the non-arising of the Mīmāṃsā and other treatises, as well as inferences such as those based on smoke.

Nor is there here the defect that the validity of perception and other means of knowledge depends on the absence of sublation; for validity, characterized as the making known of an unknown object, does not apply to errors and the like.
Furthermore, the object of an error and so forth does not exist at either the prior or subsequent time, such that it could remain in a state of being unknown.
In this very manner, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of Smṛti should be inferred.
Furthermore, for one who considers the nature of authority (*prāmāṇya*) to consist in the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*), how could there be a lack of authority for Smṛti?
No further sublation of that [cognition] is observed;
therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in accepting cognitions such as error and doubt.
That the *puruṣa* is the knower (*pramātṛ*), whose nature is eternal, ever-arisen, and objectless cognition—this is common to both the non-theistic and the theistic [Sāṃkhya systems].
In that system, the Lord (Iśvara) maintains a twofold division based on the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para);
furthermore, he determines a threefold division within the individual soul itself, based on the distinctions of gods, humans, and denizens of hell.

In both these positions, because the person (pums) is immutable (kūṭastha), it is primordial matter (prakṛti)—composed of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas—that undergoes transformation into the form of the world; and the created world consists essentially of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
And it is also approved [by others]:

the twenty-five principles (tattvas) of the atheistic [Sāṃkhya] are the person (puruṣa), primordial matter (prakṛti), the great one (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the mind (manas), the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, the nose, speech, the hand, the foot, the anus, the organ of generation, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether, wind, fire, water, and earth.
Because the Supreme Person (puruṣa) exceeds the Lord (īśvara), there are twenty-six;
as it has been said:
“Root nature (mūlaprakṛti) is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolutes;
the group of sixteen is the evolute only; and the person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolute.”
Thus,
he states the plurality of persons by means of the established order of birth, death, and so forth:
"Because of the specific determination of births, deaths, and instruments, and because of their non-simultaneous activity..."
The plurality of Puruṣas is established also from the variation in the three guṇas.
Thus:

through auspicious, inauspicious, and mixed karmas, men [experience] saṃsāra; and through the knowledge of the principles of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, they attain liberation: "By dharma there is ascent to higher realms; by adharma, descent to lower realms."
"Through knowledge, liberation is attained; through its opposite, bondage is held to occur."
And thus:
in both cases, the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and so forth, as well as the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), are dharmas characterized by engagement and withdrawal.
That which is characterized by engagement is the cause of saṃsāra.
That which is characterized by cessation is the cause of liberation through the gateway of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
This is the distinction: for the follower of the Theistic school (*seśvara*), yoga conjoined with the knowledge of reality is the cause of liberation;
for the other [the non-theist], the knowledge of reality conjoined with yoga is the cause of liberation.

The limbs of yoga are restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi).
The fruits of yoga are twofold, distinguished as knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā).
Among these, those consisting of knowledge are devotion, wisdom, and dispassion.
The eightfold sovereign powers, such as *aṇiman* and so forth, consist of ignorance;
likewise are other external yogic accomplishments (*yogasiddhis*).
As they have said:
“O Lord of Men, having attained the power of yoga, one may indeed assume many bodies for oneself and travel across the entire earth with them.”
And so forth.
Here, for the follower of the theistic school (Seśvara), liberation is the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord by the yogi through yoga conjoined with the knowledge of reality;

for the follower of the atheistic school (Nirīśvara), liberation is the attainment of the discrimination between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa) through knowledge conjoined with yoga.
Furthermore, what is the distinction of the Supreme Person from the individual knower (kṣetrajña) in the theistic position?
The Lord (īśvara) is a particular person untouched by afflictions (kleśa), karma, its fruition (vipāka), and latent dispositions (āśaya);
whereas the individual knower is one conjoined with afflictions and the like.
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the five afflictions (*kleśas*).
Action (*karman*) consists of merit and demerit.
Ripening (*vipāka*) is the fruit of action, characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion.
The disposition is the internal organ.

An Exposition of the Views of Prabhākara and Others: Although Prabhākara— who maintains that the four means of valid cognition beginning with perception (pratyakṣa) are authoritative along with presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)—

and Bhaṭṭakumāra— who maintains that there are five means of valid cognition beginning with perception along with non-existence (abhāva)— are equal in their status as commentators on the Jaiminīya Bhāṣya, they disagree regarding the knower (pramātṛ) and the object of knowledge (prameya), just as they do regarding the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
How so?
For one for whom non-existence is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is no such thing as "non-existence" that could serve as an object for that teacher.
What then? When it is said that "there is no jar on the ground," only the bare ground itself is manifested;
and darkness is merely the absence of the perception of form, not a distinct substance.
Furthermore, for one for whom existence is a means of valid cognition, there also exists for that youth an object characterized by non-existence;
and that [non-existence] is of five kinds, distinguished as absolute non-existence and so forth.
In that regard, there is the absolute non-existence of attachment in a rabbit;
there is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of jars and other things prior to their production.

Non-existence subsequent to destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is that which occurs after the disintegration [of an object]. Mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is the absence of the nature of one thing in another, such as the absence of the nature of a cloth in a jar.
[The non-existence] of lamps and so forth located within a room...
The absence [of a thing] in its own locus, such as in Maṅgaṇa and so forth, is called non-existence through relation (saṃsargābhāva).
And darkness is a distinct substance.
It is not merely the absence of light,
nor is it merely the absence of the perception of form.
Why?
Because this contradicts such scriptural passages as "There was darkness" (*tama āsīt*).
Furthermore, if darkness were the absence of light, would darkness be the absence of a single light or the absence of all lights?
In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would be perceived at all times.
Because the absence of a single light is always and everywhere possible,
in the second case [of the definition], darkness would never be perceived, since the absence of all light is impossible anywhere at all.
Thus, the position that darkness is the absence of the perception of form is also to be refuted.

If one conceives of darkness as non-existence (abhāva) despite its being perceived as a positive entity (bhāva), how could one prevent the conception of light as the non-existence of darkness? Furthermore, for a teacher who does not accept non-existence, since there is no such thing as the "absence of the perception of form," how can the claim that darkness has that nature be consistent?
If he asserts that the cognition of non-existence lacks an object, how could he possibly refute the Mādhyamika who establishes that the cognition of existence is without a basis?
Therefore, this [argument] is trivial.
As it was said by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda: "Darkness is indeed mobile, blue, and possessed of distinctions of priority and posteriority..."
Because it possesses properties different from those of well-known substances, it deserves to be distinguished from the nine [substances].
Thus,

even though the Veda is eternal and possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), there would be a lack of authority for the portions consisting of mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the Upaniṣadic portions, and the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
[Page 033]
Alternatively, its authority may be established in some way as being supplementary to ritual injunctions;
[it also asserts] the eternity of the worlds of heaven, earth, and the netherworld,
and the absence of a Supreme Lord.
The manifoldness and existence of the universe, which consists of both sentient and insentient entities;
and the fact that deities such as Indra and Agni are merely words ending in the dative case, due to the absence of a fivefold corporeal form.
The nature of Dharma as consisting of the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, Paśubandha, Soma-yāga, and other rites,
as well as the nature of liberation as the Self’s abiding in its own essential state, were no different for both Guru and Kumāra;
this much, however, was the distinction.
All cognitions of the Guru are true to reality, because cognitions such as error and doubt are merely a lack of discrimination (*aviveka*).

Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), by virtue of its apprehension of a persisting object like a jar that was previously unknown, is included within direct experience (*anubhava*) itself; thus, cognition consists of only two categories: perception and memory.
And their self-luminosity is like that of the Sāṃkhya and other schools;

for if cognition were cognizable by another cognition, there would result the fallacy of infinite regress because that [second cognition] would likewise require another, and if it were an object of knowledge, it would follow that it is not cognition, just like a jar.

However, according to the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the self is indeed a specific type of insentient substance that serves as the substratum for attributes such as cognition; for this very reason, it is distinct from the body and other such things, eternal, omnipresent, wandering through the three worlds under the influence of karma, established by means of valid cognition such as perception, and possesses its own inherent nature.
Although it is insentient, it is designated as a "knower" because it manifests as the substratum of knowledge.

Because a jar and so forth appear as objects, they possess the nature of being knowable; therefore, in the cognition "I know the jar," the Guru— who maintains the theory of the perception of the threefold complex (tripuṭī)— declares that knowledge manifests by itself, the knower manifests as its substrate, and the jar manifests as its object.
And thus says that [author]:
"The self is distinct from the intellect, the senses, and the body; it is all-pervading, eternal, manifold, and appears in each field upon the basis of objects."
Thus,
its differentiation is its very own nature, independent of anything else, and not a separate property.
For if that were the case, it would entail the undesirable consequence of requiring dependence on further distinctions.

Furthermore, the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is precisely the mandate (*niyoga*) directed toward objects such as sacrifices; because this is not accessible through other means of knowledge, it is called the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*).
It is called "kārya" (the task to be accomplished) because it is achievable through human effort (*kṛti*), and it is called "pradhāna" (the primary object) because it is the objective of that effort.
However, the fact that it bestows fruits such as heaven upon the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled), who is its own means of accomplishment, does not constitute a violation of its independence.

In this regard, in the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma," the *niyoga* (the mandate) is understood through the *liṅ* suffix in the word "yajeta" (should sacrifice), just as in a king's command: "One desiring a comfortable dwelling should worship me.
Since that [mandate] is established for someone in some particular object, the object is indicated by the verbal root (*prakṛti*) "yajati" (to sacrifice).
By the phrase "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is presented;

by the instrumental hearing (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) in the word "by means of the Agniṣṭoma," the specific sacrifice in which the injunction applies is presented; and by the qualification of the eligible person as "desiring heaven," the specific nature of the person to be enjoined is established.
Therefore, this is the meaning: there is an injunction for one desiring heaven regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Other injunctions as well are injunctions for its subsidiaries, according to the principle that "that which lacks a fruit when in proximity to something possessing a fruit is a subsidiary to it."
Mantras, as reminders for performance, possess the status of being auxiliary elements (*aṅga*).

Explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), which illuminate the excellence of the result, also assist the injunction (*vidhi*) because they induce the desire to perform the mandate (*niyoga*) that accomplishes that [result]. This same principle applies elsewhere as well.

Even regarding the teacher of teachers, Kumāra, there are various kinds of cognitions— distinguished by experience, recollection, and recognition— and even within experience itself, distinguished by being correct, erroneous, or doubtful, as in the cases of Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, Patañjali, and others.
The Knower, however, has the nature of the cognition of substance and is established by the means of valid cognition consisting of perception, inference, postulation, and scripture.
In this regard, because its intrinsic nature is distinct from that of the object of knowledge, it is not of the nature of ignorance;
and because it is the substratum of qualities such as intellect (*buddhi*), it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*).
Nor should it be argued that because the substance which is the substratum of knowledge is distinct from knowledge, a commingling with knowledge is impossible;
for we observe that even the solar orb, though distinct from light, is itself considered light by virtue of being the cause of illumination.
Furthermore, the status of the self as the object of the notion "I" cannot be established unless it possesses both inert and non-inert aspects.

Furthermore, as for the claim that erroneous cognitions consist in a lack of discrimination (*aviveka*), that is weak; for one who accepts non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) as the nature of error, it is impossible to speak of "non-discrimination" as being the absence of discrimination.
If it is argued that there is no distinction between the two acts of perception and recollection, we say no;
for an error consists in the experience of identity with the silver present before one, as in the thought "this is silver."

Therefore, for a person possessing the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a previous experience of silver, due to a defect in the instrument such as a glass lens and due to a defect in the object such as similarity, there occurs an error consisting in the manifestation of that very fragment of mother-of-pearl— which was apprehended as "this" merely as a white, shining thing— in the form of the remembered silver.
Furthermore, cognitions of jars, pleasure, and so forth, are accessible through subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*).
This is because the cognition "this is a jar" is made an object by a subsequent cognition in the form "I know the jar";
nor does this lead to an infinite regress,
because there is no further desire to know beyond the knower.
Furthermore, difference is not merely the essential nature of the thing that possesses difference;

for if it were, the word "difference" would become a synonym for words such as "pot," and moreover, it is impossible for a difference whose establishment depends upon something else to constitute the essential nature [of that thing].
Nor does the fault of requiring another distinction apply to this, because it is logically established that it brings about both itself and others, just like the self (ātman).
For he, knowing every object, knows himself as well;
and cultivation (bhāvanā) is the meaning of the injunction.
And that [cultivation] possesses three factors: what [is to be cultivated], by what [means], and in what manner.
In that context, the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) serves to fulfill the requirement of the "what" (*kim*) element;
the verbal root "to sacrifice" (*yajati*), as a constituent part of the base form, fulfills the requirement of the "by what means" (*kena*) element;
and the term "Agniṣṭoma," as a further specification of that base form, serves to illuminate its particular mode.
The third characteristic, the instrumental factor (*pratyayāṃśa*), is for the purpose of making known its status as the instrument (*karaṇatva*).
Nor is it impossible for a momentary sacrifice to be the means of accomplishing a result occurring at a later time,
because that is possible by way of a refinement (*saṃskāra*) inherent in the sacrificer.
The injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and other such rites provide the specific details as to how one should bring [the result] about.
Therefore, the meaning is this: "One who desires that [result] should bring about heaven by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
According to these two views, even liberation—characterized by the self's abiding in its own true nature—is attainable through ritual action alone.
How so?

For one who does not perform even those optional (*kāmya*) actions that have been prohibited, there is an absence of the causes consisting of merit and demerit; thus, being devoid of the resulting movements to the upper, lower, or middle worlds, he remains free from transgression. Furthermore, for the sacrificer who performs the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites and exhausts his prior auspicious and inauspicious karmas through the experience of their fruits, the state of abiding in his own true nature occurs effortlessly, even without [the cultivation of] knowledge.
This might be the case:
whether the teacher (Guru) and Kumāra are non-omniscient or omniscient, the statement that "the universe is without a Lord" would be untrustworthy.
In the first case, [they would be] of limited knowledge...
Because [the other two] are subject to destruction and because their words are deceptive,
whereas the Upaniṣadic followers maintain that he alone who is omniscient is the Lord;
thus, by those two...
Even the words of Jaimini and Śabarasvāmin, who have been examined, are indeed not to be trusted.

Now, if it is argued that by them only the Lord (īśvara) favored by the logicians was refuted, and not the one favored by the Upaniṣads which constitutes the very nature of the individual soul (kṣetrajña); [then we reply:]...

That is not so; for those who maintain that it is karma alone— not the Lord— that bestows desired and undesired fruits upon embodied beings, and who accept that the Veda is solely concerned with dharma, the nature of the Lord as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) would be rendered ineffective.
Furthermore, because it lacks establishment by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

and since the status of the Supreme Lord as an object of inference has been refuted by [the author] himself, while it has been proven that the scripture (*āgama*) is solely devoted to *dharma*, by what means of valid cognition could [the Lord] be established?
As for the liberation described as characterized by abiding in one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*):
In that regard as well, was the Self previously established in its own essential nature, or not?

In the first case, liberation cannot be achieved through ritual action (*karman*), because the fruit of action consists of origination, attainment, modification, or purification; and for that which is already established, origination and the rest are impossible.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for it is impossible to establish that a form which did not previously exist constitutes its own essential nature (*svarūpa*),
since an essential nature is defined as a form that is non-deviant.
If liberation were achievable through action, it could not be an eternal human goal,
according to the logical principle that "whatever is produced is impermanent. Furthermore,
in the doctrine of a non-conscious self, the state of absolute isolation (kaivalya) would unavoidably have to be regarded as being like a void or like a stone.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the self has the nature of the awareness of substances,
that too is incorrect;

for if one were to admit no difference between awareness and non-awareness, it would follow that even existence and non-existence, and so forth, would be identical, and it would also be untenable for cognition to be accessible through a subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*).

Because it is contradictory for that which is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) to be simultaneously the knowledge itself (*jñāna*). Furthermore, if the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) does not depend on anything else for its own establishment, then it is possible for the preceding cognition to be established in the same way.
If cognition that is itself unestablished were to illuminate its object, then the object would likewise have to illuminate the cognition, as there is no distinction between them.
Therefore, it must be accepted that all cognitions are self-luminous.

However, since these cognitions are particular modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) and are thus insentient (*jaḍa*), their nature as self-luminous cannot be logically consistent on their own; rather, they must be accepted as such solely through the proximity of the conscious Self (*cidātman*).
"Everything shines after Him alone as He shines; by His light all this is illumined"—so says the Śruti.

Furthermore, the attempt to dispel the fault of infinite regress by taking the property of difference to reside in that which possesses difference, on the grounds that it is self-explanatory (svaparanirvāhaka), is also untenable.
Because the distinction between properties such as form and taste, on the one hand, and their substrata, as well as among themselves, is not established;
indeed, it is impossible for properties to have other properties as their substrata.
Furthermore, the so-called "distinction" of all things is a single [concept].
Or is it manifold?
Even if it is one, is it insentient or non-insentient?
By the first [alternative], this non-insentient [consciousness] would exist within the self.
Because the connection between the seer and the seen is impossible;

as for the second [alternative], it would follow that the very self (ātman) is the referent of the word "difference," since that is the defining characteristic of a single, all-pervading, non-insentient reality.
If it is insentient, does it depend on some other distinction, or does it not depend on anything?
If it depends [on another], there is an infinite regress.
If it does not depend on difference, then even the distinct entities themselves would be non-distinct, just like the absence of difference.
Therefore, difference cannot be established— whether as an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) or as a property (*dharma*)— even by Śakra himself.
How can there be a distinction between the proliferation of the sentient and the insentient? Or how can there be a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)?
Therefore, even the doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas should not be accepted by those desiring the highest good; thus, the doctrine of the proponents of Brahman is introduced.
The exponents of Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ) are also of two kinds:
the followers of the Upaniṣads (aupaniṣadāḥ) and the followers of the Purāṇas (paurāṇikāḥ).
The followers of the Upaniṣads are also of two kinds: those who prioritize Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma) and those who prioritize Brahman without attributes (nirguṇa-brahma).
In this regard, Rāmānuja and others primarily emphasize Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahman),
whereas the venerable Ācārya [Śaṅkara] and others primarily emphasize Brahman without attributes (nirguṇa-brahman).
The exposition of the doctrine of those who maintain that Brahman possesses attributes (*saguṇabrahmavāda*):
among them, for those established in the qualified [Brahman], the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and the world (*jagat*) is indeed real.
Furthermore, *māyā*, which is the cause thereof, is also real because it is the power (*śakti*) of the Blessed Lord.
Because the existence of potencies within sesame seeds and the like is observed,
that [power] is designated as "māyā" on account of its capacity to bring about the production of what was previously unproduced,
not because it is a non-entity.

According to the Vedic revelation, "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion" (*indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate*), there exists a distinction of that [Supreme Being] for each individual soul; thus, in age after age, those seeking liberation, performing with devotion and faith the hearing, chanting, meditation, and worship of the Blessed Lord— who consists of the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) known as Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha— attain, by the grace of the Blessed Lord, [the goal].

Having transcended that Māyā which is the cause of birth and the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), they desire liberation characterized by Sālokya, Sārūpya, Sāmīpya, and Sāyujya, in accordance with their service.
However, those devoid of the Lord’s grace, deluded by that Māyā, continue to wander here in saṃsāra; such is the summary of the established doctrine (siddhānta).
As it has been stated by the authors of the Śārīraka-saṅgraha:

"Many ignorant souls of immeasurable forms, though desiring liberation, [stray] due to their reliance on both knowledge and ignorance; and for them, according to the age, [you provide] the supreme good.

Yet some of little learning, with minds obstructed by the hostility of gods, have fabricated the notion that *māyā*—which arises from the Lord and follows [him]—is that which increases worldly existence."
Thus,

the learned have declared that the opinion of those whose minds are subject to the destruction wrought by fate and who possess little learning is to be disregarded, because it is rooted in the delusion regarding the world, the individual soul, and the Lord, which are not real entities.
An Exposition of the Doctrine of the Attributeless Brahman (Nirguṇa-brahma-vāda):

For the followers of the Upaniṣads and the Purāṇas— beginning with the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda— who hold that the attributeless Brahman is primary and who maintain six or eight types of means of valid cognition, the ultimate reality is, in truth, only the single principle of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (sac-cid-ānanda) Brahman.
And that [consciousness] is not accessible through other means of knowledge (*māna*),

because the entire universe— consisting of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*)— is superimposed upon it and thus lacks existence apart from it, and because it is inherently insentient (*jaḍa*) and its manifestation is dependent upon that [consciousness].
Even that non-existence could not manifest without depending upon the conscious self,
because its nature is non-luminous;
how much more so, then, positive entities such as jars, cloths, and the like?
If the self alone is the reality,
and if it is an undivided entity,
from where does this duality consisting of the world, the individual soul, and the Lord appear?
If that [consciousness] were not a real entity and not unitary,
how much less could the universe appear?
Indeed, without relying on a single reality that is self-luminous, it is impossible to establish the existence of the manifold, insentient universe.
If duality were absolutely non-existent, then from where would the appearance of existence arise?
We say it is by means of the existence of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-sattā*).
Just as there is the appearance of the cognition of the existence of silver due to the existence of mother-of-pearl:

for that [mother-of-pearl], although known merely as this white, shining object, being unknown in its own true form, appears to a person possessing the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the experience of silver as having the nature of an appearance of silver manifested by one's own ignorance.
It shines forth;

likewise, although the Self is known as the mere substance of luminosity in the form "I am," it remains unknown in its own true nature consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). Thus, being ignorant, the Self perceives within itself the manifold expansion of duality (*bhedaprapañca*)—consisting of the world, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the Lord (*īśvara*)—which is the manifestation of the ignorance of the Self (*ātmāvidyā*).
Even in this position, from the standpoint of conventional reality (*vyavahāra*), there are two categories: the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*).
Among these, the seen is *māyā*.
The seer is the Puruṣa who presides over that [Māyā];
and Māyā is not real, because it is other than the real Self.
Because it is the cause of the world, which is false like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and because it is sublated by the knowledge of the true nature of its substrate;
nor is it non-existent, because it is the cause of the entire universe.
Furthermore, because it is directly perceived, one cannot say "I do not know myself.
Nor can it be both existent and non-existent, because existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive in nature and thus cannot coexist in a single substratum.
By process of elimination, it follows that it is indeterminable;
and furthermore, it is not distinct from the self,
because [if it were], non-apprehension would result.
Furthermore, it would follow that [the self] is absolutely non-existent;
nor is it non-different [from consciousness], because identity between the insentient and the sentient is impossible.
Nor is it both different and non-different,
because difference and non-difference, being by nature mutually exclusive, cannot logically coexist in one place without dispute.
Nor is it composed of parts.
Because it would follow that [the cause] is an effect;
nor is it partless,
because it undergoes transformation into the entire universe.
Nor is it of both forms, because that would involve a contradiction.
Therefore, Māyā is simply a certain power of the Supreme Self, delightful only so long as it is not investigated;
and she consists of the three guṇas.
The qualities (guṇas) are sattva, rajas, and tamas.
And the nature of Māyā is such because it is observed that its effect, the world, consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and so it is stated in scripture.
This very [Māyā] is called "ignorance" (avidyā) in some places, "primordial matter" (prakṛti) in some, "the Imperishable" (akṣara) in some, "power" (śakti) in some, and "delusion" (moha) in others.

The Vedāntins maintain that from the Self endowed with those [powers], the five elements beginning with space arise, and from those elements presided over by the conscious Self, the collective and individual bodies are produced. The Paurāṇikas, however, hold that the appearance of sound occurs through the very existence of the substrate of duality,
just as [the appearance] of silver [occurs].
In this view, at the level of conventional discourse, there are two categories: the seer and the seen;
the seen is illusion (*māyā*).
The Puruṣa is the Seer.
Māyā is indeed the power (śakti) of the Supreme Self, which is delightful only so long as it is not investigated.
And she consists of the three guṇas and is one, according to such scriptural passages as "the one unborn [female]" (ajāmekām).
The scriptural mention of their multiplicity in the passage "Indra by means of his *māyās*" is due solely to the distinction between its parts;
this very [power] is designated by such terms as "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
From the Self endowed with that [power], ether and the other elements are born.
The Vedāntins maintain that from these [subtle elements], bodies in both collective (samaṣṭi) and individual (vyaṣṭi) forms arise.
Now, the exposition of the Paurāṇika view:
the Paurāṇikas, however, hold that from the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is variegated by Māyā, the Great One (mahat) arises.
From Mahat arises the ego (ahaṃkāra),
and it is threefold in form according to the distinctions of the powers of substance, cognition, and action.
Among these, from the ego characterized by tamas (tāmasāhaṃkāra) arise the subtle elements (tanmātra) of sound and so forth, as well as the gross elements (bhūta) such as space and the rest.
From the *sāttvika* ego, through the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), the deities of the fourteen organs beginning with the directions, as well as the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), are born.
From the *rājasa* ego, through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), the sense organs beginning with hearing and the organs of action beginning with speech are born.
These elements, from Mahat down to the earth, impelled by the Puruṣa who possesses Māyā, combine with one another and initiate the golden cosmic egg (*haima-brahmāṇḍa*).
In that regard, there are fourteen worlds and four types of bodies;
and into those bodies, the conscious self (cidātman), which is the primary cause of all, enters as both witness (sākṣin) and as the one possessing ego-identification (abhimānin).
The witness is the Supreme Lord (parameśvara).
The individual soul (jīva) is characterized by ego-inflation,
according to such scriptural passages as "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) and "The Lord of all beings" (*īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām*).
And because of such Smṛti passages as these,
in either of these two views, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) consists of the effects of Māyā characterized as the elements and elemental derivatives;
the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are six, beginning with perception, or eight.
The individual soul (*jīva*) is the cognizer.
It is accessible through perception and inference, and it is differentiated in each body by means of *māyā*.
The Supreme Lord, by means of the authority of scripture supported by inference— also known as *tarka*— is established as being by nature eternally pure,

conscious, and free; he is omniscient and omnipotent, and through the fivefold activities characterized by the creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace of the universe, he sports within his own self by means of *māyā*, which consists of the three *guṇas*.
Remaining as one alone in all fields, he governs all the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas);
nor is there an impossibility of the relationship between the governed and the governor in a single entity,
because that is possible by resorting to the distinctions of māyā.
Thus, the entire manifold of duality consists of illusion (māyā);
from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), only non-dual Brahman exists.
Since, according to these two views, bondage is rooted in ignorance (avidyā), liberation is simply the cessation of that [ignorance].
And since the scripture, beginning with "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," reiterates the vision of the Self and prescribes hearing and other means as its instruments,
for a person endowed with the means such as discrimination who engages in the hearing of the Vedānta and so forth, [this occurs] through the hearing of the Lord’s deeds and the like.

When there arises the direct realization of the identity of the individual self and the Supreme Self—namely, "I am Brahman"—in one whose inner organ has been purified, everything becomes accomplished without blemish.
